articles.title: Building a Locale Switcher That Respects hreflang and User Choice
articles.excerpt: Language switchers look trivial: a dropdown with flags. In practice they are where many multilingual sites break their own SEO and annoy users at the same time. This post outlines a switcher design th…
articles.body: Language switchers look trivial: a dropdown with flags. In practice they are where many multilingual sites break their own SEO and annoy users at the same time. This post outlines a switcher design that keeps search engines and humans happy, with small code samples. Principles Every language version has its own URL ( /en/ , /de/ , /ja/ ). The switcher links to the equivalent page, not the homepage of the other language. Automatic detection suggests, it never forces a redirect. A user's explicit choice is remembered. Generate links from the same map as hreflang Keep one data structure that lists equivalents for each page, and use it both for <link rel="alternate" hreflang> tags and for the switcher. If they come from different sources, they will drift.

articles.title: Reconciling Crypto Gateway Settlement Reports Against Your Orders With pandas
articles.excerpt: Finance teams at merchants who accept crypto usually ask the same question at month end: does the money that reached the bank match the orders we shipped? A crypto gateway that converts to USD and pay…
articles.body: Finance teams at merchants who accept crypto usually ask the same question at month end: does the money that reached the bank match the orders we shipped? A crypto gateway that converts to USD and pays out to a bank account produces a settlement report, your store produces an order export, and the bank produces a statement. This post shows a small pandas script that joins the three and flags the differences, so a human only reviews the exceptions. The three inputs Order export from your store or billing system: order ID, customer currency amount, currency, status, created time. Gateway settlement report : invoice ID, your order ID (passed as metadata when creating the invoice), crypto asset, network, crypto amount received, USD value at confirmation, fee, net amount, payout batch ID.

articles.title: How do AI agents authenticate? (The problem nobody has solved yet)
articles.excerpt: If you've built an MCP server or an API that agents call, you've run into this problem. Your agent needs to call a tool. That tool needs to know who's calling. So you do what everyone does: generate a…
articles.body: If you've built an MCP server or an API that agents call, you've run into this problem. Your agent needs to call a tool. That tool needs to know who's calling. So you do what everyone does: generate an API key, paste it in an env var, and move on. It works. Until it doesn't. The key gets committed to a repo. Or it gets shared across a whole team's agents, so every agent looks identical in your logs. Or someone leaves and you realize you have no idea which credentials they had. Or you're running 50 agents and managing 50 sets of credentials per tool. This isn't a process problem. It's an architectural one. API keys were designed for humans. They were never designed for machines.

articles.body: It came from outer space, exploding high above the South Atlantic off the coast of Argentina. That April 1 event — an incoming meteor , also termed a bolide — was observed by both U.S. space-based military and civil sensors. Hush-hush U.S. government satellite sensors detected the speedy fireball cutting through our atmosphere. The object's brightness peaked at an altitude of nearly 60 miles (90.5 kilometers) over the South Atlantic. That dazzling spectacle was also caught by the National Atmospheric and Oceanic Administration's GOES-E and Europe's Meteosat Third Generation (MTG) Imager-1 satellite. Those two independent spacecraft in geostationary orbit detected the bolide via onboard lightning imagers.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 1, 1962: The Soviet Union Launches Mars 1 spacecraft to Red Planet during the Space Race
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 1, 1962, the Soviet Union launched the Mars 1 spacecraft on a mission to fly by the Red Planet. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 1, 1962, the Soviet Union launched the Mars 1 spacecraft on a mission to fly by the Red Planet. While it did end up flying by Mars , the mission was not exactly a success. After it separated from the rocket, it deployed its solar panels and started cruising toward Mars. When mission controllers were checking out the telemetry it transmitted back to Earth, they found out that Mars 1 had sprung a leak in one of the gas valves that controls the spacecraft's orientation. And without a working orientation system, Mars 1 would have a hard time pointing its antennas in the right direction. It lost contact with Earth when it was about halfway to Mars . A model of Mars 1, a Mars flyby spacecraft launched to the Red Planet by the Soviet Union on Nov. 1, 1962.

articles.title: Anthropic VS code extension on Cursor backdoored for nearly 12 hours
articles.excerpt: It's still unknown how attackers got access to Anthropic's verified Cursor account.
articles.body: An official extension for Anthropic’s Claude model was backdoored and threatened as many as 5,000 developers' machines, multiple sources reported Friday. Anthropic so far has yet to warn customers of the incident. The compromised package was a VS Code extension available in the marketplace of Cursor, a maker of AI-assisted developer tools, the company said Friday. The malicious version, 2.1.313, subsequently affected “at most 5,000 users,” presumably when they either downloaded it or their systems automatically fetched and installed it. Anthropic pushed version 2.1.314 several hours after the previous version became available on Cursor, according to independent researcher Kevin Beaumont.
